   - “APT38 Ronin Bridge theft attribution Lazarus”

7. The searches returned the same four source records in the immutable benchmark snapshot. The retrieved excerpts were explicitly marked as truncated. No separate directly retrievable FBI, OFAC, DOJ, Ronin operator, or Harmony operator source record was returned with a distinct source ID.

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## 1. Scope and source limitations

The retrieved evidence consists of three private-sector blockchain-intelligence or investigative sources and one Elliptic resource record whose displayed content was primarily a general Elliptic insights page rather than a substantive Harmony-specific report:

- Elliptic’s Ronin analysis: **SRC-003**
- Chainalysis’s Ronin analysis: **SRC-002**
- Elliptic’s Harmony analysis reporting an FBI confirmation: **SRC-001**
- Elliptic’s “The Harmony Horizon Bridge Hack” resource page: **SRC-004**

The search results did **not** return separate source IDs for:

- The FBI statement itself concerning Harmony;
- The OFAC sanctions record itself concerning the Ronin exploiter address;
- A DOJ indictment, complaint, forfeiture action, or court document concerning either theft;
- An official Ronin Network postmortem with transaction hashes or wallet addresses;
- An official Harmony/Horizon Bridge postmortem with transaction hashes or wallet addresses;
- An APT38-specific attribution statement.

Accordingly, statements about FBI confirmation and OFAC sanctions are preserved as reported by Elliptic in **SRC-001** and **SRC-003**, rather than presented as direct quotations from the underlying FBI or OFAC records.

The retrieved excerpts did not provide wallet addresses, transaction hashes, named wallet clusters, infrastructure indicators, malware names, or exchange deposit addresses. No such identifiers are added here.

## 2. March 2022 Ronin Bridge theft

### 2.1 Theft event, date, assets, and amounts

Elliptic reported:

> “On March 29th, the Ronin Network announced that 173,600 Ether (ETH) and 25.5 million USD Coins had been stolen from the Ronin cross-chain bridge six days earlier.” **[SRC-003]**

The same source stated:

> “The total value of the stolen cryptoassets at the time of the theft was $540 million. This is the second largest crypto theft of all time.” **[SRC-003]**

The source further stated:

> “The incident occurred six days before the exploit was announced by Ronin.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic reported that, amid confusion over the delayed response, Ronin announced:

> “the exploit was only discovered after a 5,000 ETH withdrawal attempt from one of their users failed.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic stated:

> “At the time of discovery, the stolen funds were worth over $615 million.” **[SRC-003]**

Chainalysis described the incident as:

> “the March 2022 theft of more than $600 million from Ronin Network, a sidechain built for the play-to-earn game Axie Infinity.” **[SRC-002]**

The amounts explicitly supported in the retrieved sources are therefore:

- **173,600 ETH**
- **25.5 million USDC**
- **$540 million** total value at the time of theft, according to Elliptic;
- **More than $600 million**, according to Chainalysis;
- **Over $615 million** at the time of discovery, according to Elliptic.

The difference between the reported dollar amounts is not resolved in the retrieved material and reflects different valuation times or descriptions.

### 2.2 Attack mechanism and operator postmortem

Elliptic stated:

> “According to a postmortem published by Ronin, the theft came as a result of an attacker hacking the ‘validator nodes’of the Ronin bridge.” **[SRC-003]**

The source explained:

> “Funds can be moved out if five of the nine validators approve it.” **[SRC-003]**

It further stated:

> “The attacker managed to get hold of the private cryptographic keys belonging to five of the validators, which was enough to steal the cryptoassets.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic reported that the Ronin postmortem claimed:

> “all evidence points to this attack being socially engineered, rather than a technical flaw” **[SRC-003]**

Chainalysis similarly stated:

> “The attack began when the Lazarus Group gained access to five of the nine private keys held by transaction validators for Ronin Network’s cross-chain bridge.” **[SRC-002]**

Chainalysis stated that the attackers:

> “used this majority to approve two transactions, both withdrawals: one for 173,600 ether (ETH) and the other for 25.5 million USD Coin (USDC).” **[SRC-002]**

The retrieved sources do not provide the validator addresses, private-key details, transaction hashes, or the exact Ronin postmortem URL or source ID.

### 2.3 Ronin attribution to Lazarus Group

Elliptic’s article title was:

> “North Korea’s Lazarus Group identified as exploiters behind $540 million Ronin bridge heist” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic reported:

> “On April 14th, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new sanctions against the thief's Ethereum address and listed the owner of this address as Lazarus Group – the North Korean state hacking group.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic stated that the sanctions:

> “prohibit US persons and entities from transacting with this address to ensure the state-sponsored group can’t cash out any further funds they continue to hold onto through US-based crypto exchanges.” **[SRC-003]**

The direct OFAC source was not separately retrieved. The retrieved evidence is therefore Elliptic’s account of the OFAC action, not the underlying OFAC record itself.

Elliptic characterized the attribution as based on several similarities:

> “Many features of the attack mirrored the method used by Lazarus Group in previous high-profile attacks, including the location of the victim, the attack method (believed to have involved social engineering) and the laundering pattern utilized by the group after the event.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic also stated:

> “It is somewhat unsurprising that this attack has been attributed to North Korea.” **[SRC-003]**

Chainalysis presented the attribution as follows:

> “Much of the value stolen from DeFi protocols can be attributed to bad actors affiliated with North Korea, especially elite hacking units like Lazarus Group.” **[SRC-002]**

It described its estimate:

> “We estimate that so far in 2022, North Korea-linked groups have stolen approximately $1 billion of cryptocurrency from DeFi protocols.” **[SRC-002]**

Chainalysis stated specifically:

> “Lazarus Group has replicated this process with large portions of Ronin’s stolen funds.” **[SRC-002]**

The retrieved sources support a public attribution of the Ronin theft to **Lazarus Group** and to a **North Korea-linked/state-sponsored actor**, with the strongest formal provenance reported by Elliptic being the alleged April 14 OFAC designation of the thief’s Ethereum address.

### 2.4 Ronin laundering and fund movement

Elliptic stated:

> “Elliptic’s internal analysis indicates that the attacker has managed to launder 18% of their stolen funds as of April 14th.” **[SRC-003]**

The reported sequence began with the stolen USDC:

> “First, the stolen USDC was swapped for ETH through decentralized exchanges (DEXs) to prevent it from being seized.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic explained the reason:

> “Tokens such as stablecoins are controlled by their issuers, who in some cases can freeze tokens involved in illicit activity.” **[SRC-003]**

It stated:

> “By converting the tokens at DEXs, the hacker avoided the anti-money laundering (AML) and 'know your customer' (KYC) checks performed at centralized exchanges.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic characterized this as:

> “an increasingly common tactic seen in hacks of this type” **[SRC-003]**

The source then reported:

> “the attacker then began laundering $16.7 million worth of ETH through three centralized exchanges.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic assessed this strategy as:

> “uncommon for typical DeFi exploits given these exchanges’ AML obligations, though it has been observed more often in past Lazarus group-affiliated exploits.” **[SRC-003]**

After the exchanges announced cooperation with law enforcement:

> “the attacker changed their laundering strategy to instead make use of Tornado Cash – a popular smart contract-based mixer on the Ethereum blockchain.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic reported:

> “Ongoing transactions have so far sent $80.3 million worth of ETH through Tornado Cash.” **[SRC-003]**

The source also stated:

> “The attacker’s blockchain activity shows that another $9.7 million worth of ETH is in intermediary wallets prepared to be laundered, most likely also through Tornado Cash.” **[SRC-003]**

It stated:

> “This leaves a considerable $433 million remaining in the attacker’s original wallet.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic said:

> “Elliptic investigators are tracking these stolen funds, and have labelled the addresses associated to this attacker in our systems – ensuring that our clients will be alerted if they receive any of these funds.” **[SRC-003]**

Chainalysis reported that:

> “The laundering of these funds has leveraged over 12,000 different crypto addresses to-date, which demonstrates the hackers’ highly sophisticated laundering capabilities.” **[SRC-002]**

Chainalysis described a typical North Korea-linked DeFi laundering process as having approximately five stages:

> “Stolen Ether sent to intermediary wallets  
> Ether mixed in batches using Tornado Cash  
> Ether swapped for bitcoin  
> Bitcoin mixed in batches  
> Bitcoin deposited to crypto-to-fiat services for cashout” **[SRC-002]**

Chainalysis stated that the Lazarus Group replicated this process with large portions of the Ronin funds. **[SRC-002]**

Chainalysis also reported that the U.S. Treasury’s OFAC sanctioned Tornado Cash:

> “for its role in laundering over $455 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Axie Infinity.” **[SRC-002]**

Following the sanctions:

> “Lazarus Group has moved away from the popular Ethereum mixer, instead leveraging DeFi services to chain hop, or switch between several different kinds of cryptocurrencies in a single transaction.” **[SRC-002]**

Chainalysis stated:

> “Bridges serve an important function to move digital assets between chains and most usage of these platforms is completely legitimate. Lazarus appears to be using bridges in an attempt to obscure source of funds.” **[SRC-002]**

The source gave an example:

> “the hacker bridged ETH from the Ethereum blockchain to the BNB chain and then swapped that ETH for USDD, which was then bridged to the BitTorrent chain.” **[SRC-002]**

Chainalysis stated:

> “Lazarus Group carried out hundreds of similar transactions across several blockchains to launder the funds they stole from Axie Infinity, in addition to the more conventional Tornado Cash-based laundering we covered above.” **[SRC-002]**

Chainalysis reported that more than $30 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen by North Korean-linked hackers had been seized, with law-enforcement and industry cooperation. **[SRC-002]**

It stated that the seizures:

> “represent approximately 10% of the total funds stolen from Axie Infinity (accounting for price differences between time stolen and seized)” **[SRC-002]**

The source stated that Chainalysis’s incident-response team:

> “utiliz[ed] advanced tracing techniques to follow stolen funds to cash out points and liaising with law enforcement and industry players to quickly freeze funds.” **[SRC-002]**

The retrieved excerpt does not identify the three centralized exchanges, the crypto-to-fiat services, the Tornado Cash deposit or withdrawal addresses, the BNB or BitTorrent bridge contracts, or any transaction hashes.

## 3. June 2022 Harmony Horizon Bridge theft

### 3.1 Theft event, date, and amount

Elliptic’s Harmony attribution article stated:

> “Horizon – a cross-chain bridge servicing the Harmony blockchain – was exploited on June 24th 2022 for $99.7 million.” **[SRC-001]**

The article title described the event as:

> “FBI confirms North Korea’s Lazarus Group as hackers behind $100 million Harmony Horizon Bridge theft” **[SRC-001]**

The source stated:

> “The FBI has confirmed that the Lazarus Group – a cyberhacker group backed by North Korea – was behind the June 2022 hack of Harmony’s Horizon Bridge.” **[SRC-001]**

The explicitly supported amounts are therefore:

- **$99.7 million**, according to the body of Elliptic’s article;
- **$100 million**, according to the article title and description.

The retrieved evidence does not provide a separate asset-by-asset breakdown for the Harmony theft.

### 3.2 FBI attribution provenance

Elliptic stated:

> “The FBI has confirmed that the Lazarus Group – a cyberhacker group backed by North Korea – was behind the June 2022 hack of Harmony’s Horizon Bridge.” **[SRC-001]**

Elliptic described this as confirming its prior assessment:

> “The announcement confirms Elliptic’s previous attribution of the $100 million hack to North Korea, which we were the first to identify after numerous similarities were observed with Lazarus’ past blockchain laundering patterns.” **[SRC-001]**

The direct FBI announcement was not returned as a separate source ID. The exact wording of the FBI’s underlying statement, its date, and its URL are therefore absent from the retrieved record.

### 3.3 Harmony attack surface and social engineering assessment

Elliptic stated:

> “Concerns had previously been raised that the bridge was over-centralized, meaning that it was particularly vulnerable to social engineering attacks – a common attack vector for the Lazarus Group.” **[SRC-001]**

Elliptic compared the Harmony event with Ronin:

> “Similar issues resulted in the criminal organization stealing over $540 million from another cross-chain bridge called Ronin earlier in March 2022.” **[SRC-001]**

This is a comparison and analytical assessment by Elliptic. The retrieved sources do not provide an official Harmony postmortem, details of compromised keys or signers, malware indicators, phishing infrastructure, or other operational evidence for the Harmony intrusion.

## 4. Harmony laundering and fund movement

Elliptic stated:

> “After stealing the funds from Horizon, the Lazarus Group then programmatically structured transactions through Tornado Cash, which is a decentralized Ethereum-based mixer.” **[SRC-001]**

Elliptic reported:

> “Elliptic researchers identified that the laundering methods employed mirrored those the Lazarus Group had used when attempting to conceal funds from the Ronin Bridge hack, which had also been sent through Tornado Cash.” **[SRC-001]**

Elliptic stated that the U.S. sanctions context involved Tornado Cash:

> “Tornado Cash was subsequently sanctioned by the US Treasury in August 2022, with Secretary of State Anthony Blinken citing its prolific use by the Lazarus Group to launder funds from its past hacks.” **[SRC-001]**

Elliptic’s research estimate was:

> “the Lazarus Group sent more than $555 million through Tornado Cash from these hacks, including more than $468 million from the Ronin hack and $96 million from the Harmony hack.” **[SRC-001]**

The source stated:

> “This North Korea-linked activity accounts for approximately 5.8% of the nearly $9 billion in total funds sent through the Tornado Cash mixer to date.” **[SRC-001]**

Elliptic said:

> “Elliptic has traced the stolen funds from the Horizon hack through Tornado Cash.” **[SRC-001]**

The article stated that:

> “The post-Tornado withdrawals were initially placed into several addresses, where they remained dormant until January 2023.” **[SRC-001]**

It then reported:

> “In January 2023, Lazarus began structuring the funds into several deposits into a privacy-based DeFi protocol called Railgun, which functions similar to a mixer.” **[SRC-001]**

Elliptic characterized Railgun as:

> “a prime alternative to Tornado Cash following sanctions against the latter.” **[SRC-001]**

Elliptic’s research further suggested:

> “a significant portion of funds – estimated at around 70% – that has been sent through Railgun to date are funds from the Harmony hack.” **[SRC-001]**

Elliptic interpreted this as suggesting:

> “that since the OFAC sanctions on Tornado Cash, North Korea may be turning to lower obfuscating services as an alternative.” **[SRC-001]**

Elliptic stated that the large share of Harmony funds in Railgun reduced the effectiveness of the mixing:

> “the fact that funds from the Harmony hack comprised such a substantial volume of the Ether passing through Railgun renders the mixing ineffective.” **[SRC-001]**

The source used the following analogy:

> “imagine if you threw five pennies into a jar full of 100 pennies, it would be extremely difficult for someone to determine which pennies were yours. However, if you threw 70 pennies into a jar with only 30 other pennies in it, then there would be a higher chance of linking those 70 specific pennies back to you.” **[SRC-001]**

Elliptic explained:

> “Mixers work in a similar way: when the anonymity set – or volume of other funds in the mixer is low – it makes the mixer less effective at concealing disproportionately large funds transfers.” **[SRC-001]**

On subsequent movement, Elliptic stated:

> “On-chain data shows that after sending the funds through Railgun, the Lazarus Group has since deposited funds into three cryptoasset exchanges.” **[SRC-001]**

The source identified two of the exchanges:

> “Two, namely Binance and Huobi, have announced that they have identified, blocked and seized a portion of the funds.” **[SRC-001]**

The third exchange was not named in the retrieved excerpt.

The retrieved source does not provide the Harmony theft’s initial wallet address, Tornado Cash transaction hashes, Railgun transaction hashes, exchange deposit addresses, or the identities of the “several addresses” used for post-Tornado withdrawals.

## 5. Comparison of laundering and fund-movement patterns

### 5.1 Similarities explicitly stated by sources

Elliptic explicitly linked the laundering patterns of the two incidents:

> “Elliptic researchers identified that the laundering methods employed mirrored those the Lazarus Group had used when attempting to conceal funds from the Ronin Bridge hack, which had also been sent through Tornado Cash.” **[SRC-001]**

The explicitly reported common features are:

- Use of **Tornado Cash**, described as a decentralized Ethereum-based mixer, after the Harmony theft and also in the Ronin laundering;
- **Programmatic structuring** of transactions through Tornado Cash in the Harmony case;
- A laundering pattern that Elliptic said **mirrored** the pattern used for Ronin;
- Subsequent use of **Railgun** for Harmony-related funds after the Tornado Cash sanctions;
- The broader use of **DeFi services and bridges for chain hopping**, explicitly described by Chainalysis for Ronin/Axie Infinity funds.

Elliptic’s Ronin report stated that similarities included:

> “the location of the victim, the attack method (believed to have involved social engineering) and the laundering pattern utilized by the group after the event.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic’s Harmony report stated that the Horizon bridge had centralization concerns and was vulnerable to social engineering, which it described as a common Lazarus attack vector. **[SRC-001]**

### 5.2 Ronin-specific laundering details

The retrieved Ronin-specific laundering evidence includes:

- Stolen USDC swapped for ETH through DEXs;
- Avoidance of stablecoin freezing risk;
- Avoidance of centralized-exchange AML/KYC controls through DEX use;
- $16.7 million in ETH sent through three centralized exchanges;
- A subsequent shift to Tornado Cash after exchanges announced cooperation with law enforcement;
- $80.3 million in ETH sent through Tornado Cash as of the date of Elliptic’s analysis;
- $9.7 million in intermediary wallets prepared for likely Tornado Cash laundering;
- $433 million remaining in the original wallet at that point;
- More than 12,000 addresses used in laundering according to Chainalysis;
- A five-stage pattern involving intermediary wallets, Tornado Cash, ETH-to-BTC conversion, Bitcoin mixing, and crypto-to-fiat cashout;
- Later chain hopping involving Ethereum, BNB Chain, USDD, and BitTorrent Chain;
- Hundreds of similar cross-chain transactions according to Chainalysis.

All of these statements are source-specific assessments or reported observations, not independently confirmed court findings in the retrieved material. **[SRC-002] [SRC-003]**

### 5.3 Harmony-specific laundering details

The retrieved Harmony-specific laundering evidence includes:

- Programmatic structuring through Tornado Cash;
- An asserted laundering pattern mirroring the Ronin laundering;
- More than $96 million attributed by Elliptic’s estimate to Harmony funds sent through Tornado Cash;
- Post-Tornado withdrawals placed into several addresses and dormant until January 2023;
- Structuring into several Railgun deposits beginning in January 2023;
- An estimate that approximately 70% of funds sent through Railgun to date were Harmony funds;
- Deposits into three cryptoasset exchanges after Railgun;
- Binance and Huobi identifying, blocking, and seizing part of the funds.

These are Elliptic’s blockchain-analysis findings and estimates as presented in **SRC-001**. The retrieved material does not provide a complete transaction-by-transaction reconstruction.

### 5.4 What the retrieved sources do not establish

The sources do not establish, through a directly retrieved primary record:

- That the same personnel conducted both thefts;
- That the two operations were coordinated;
- That one theft funded or enabled the other;
- That the same wallet cluster was used in both attacks;
- That the same malware, phishing kit, domain, server, exchange account, or operational infrastructure was used;
- That the two incidents shared a specific transaction hash or wallet address;
- That APT38 was responsible for either theft;
- That Lazarus Group and APT38 are identical organizational designations in relation to these particular incidents.

The reported similarities in laundering patterns support an analytical comparison and are explicitly used by Elliptic in attributing Harmony to Lazarus Group, but the retrieved sources do not support a stronger claim of operational identity or direct relationship between the two thefts.

## 6. Lazarus Group and APT38

### 6.1 Lazarus Group

The retrieved sources explicitly use the following descriptions:

- Elliptic described Lazarus Group as “the North Korean state hacking group.” **[SRC-003]**
- Elliptic described Lazarus Group as “a cyberhacker group backed by North Korea.” **[SRC-001]**
- Chainalysis described Lazarus Group as an “elite hacking unit” associated with North Korea-linked groups. **[SRC-002]**

The Ronin theft is attributed to Lazarus Group through Elliptic’s report that OFAC listed the thief’s Ethereum address as owned by Lazarus Group. **[SRC-003]**

The Harmony theft is attributed to Lazarus Group through Elliptic’s report that the FBI confirmed Lazarus Group was behind the hack. **[SRC-001]**

### 6.2 APT38

The retrieved sources do **not** mention **APT38** in the displayed excerpts. No source returned by the research system explicitly attributes either the Ronin theft or the Harmony Horizon Bridge theft to APT38.

No relationship between Lazarus Group and APT38 is established by the retrieved source records for these incidents.

## 7. Sanctions, seizures, and exchange activity

### 7.1 Ronin

Elliptic reported that on April 14, OFAC announced sanctions against the thief’s Ethereum address and listed its owner as Lazarus Group. **[SRC-003]**

Chainalysis reported:

> “more than $30 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen by North Korean-linked hackers has been seized.” **[SRC-002]**

It stated that this was:

> “the first time ever that cryptocurrency stolen by a North Korean hacking group has been seized” **[SRC-002]**

Chainalysis attributed the seizures to collaboration among law enforcement, the Axie Infinity team, and cryptocurrency-industry organizations. **[SRC-002]**

### 7.2 Harmony

Elliptic reported that Binance and Huobi announced that they had identified, blocked, and seized a portion of Harmony-related funds after the Railgun activity. **[SRC-001]**

The retrieved material does not state the exact amount seized by Binance or Huobi, the third exchange’s identity, or the relevant deposit addresses or hashes.

## 8. Other contextual assessments in the retrieved sources

Elliptic stated that Lazarus Group had targeted crypto entities since at least 2017. **[SRC-003]**

It stated:

> “Until 2021, the majority of this activity was directed towards centralized exchanges located in South Korea or elsewhere in Asia. However, within the past year the group’s attention has turned to DeFi services.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic noted that although Ronin Network’s bridge was decentralized:

> “the creators of the network Sky Mavis are located in Vietnam.” **[SRC-003]**

Elliptic stated:

> “Many commentators believe that cryptoassets stolen by Lazarus Group are used to fund the state’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs.” **[SRC-003]**

It also stated:

> “With recent reports that North Korea may be again preparing for nuclear testing, today’s sanctions activity highlights the importance of ensuring that Lazarus Group is not able to successfully launder the proceeds of these attacks.” **[SRC-003]**

Chainalysis stated that cryptocurrency’s transparency enabled investigators to follow the funds and disrupt cybercrime activity. **[SRC-002]**

It contrasted blockchain tracing with traditional financial channels:

> “This would never be possible in traditional financial channels, where money laundering usually involves networks of shell companies and financial institutions in jurisdictions that may not cooperate.” **[SRC-002]**

Chainalysis stated:

> “Much of the funds stolen from Axie Infinity remain unspent in cryptocurrency wallets under” **[SRC-002]**

The retrieved excerpt ends at that point and does not include the remainder of the sentence.

---
